To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we propose several new models for deep document relevance ranking, and that these models outperform BM25, DRMM and PACRR on two datasets.

we have proposed several models for document relevance matching that incorporate context-sensitive representations of terms, and that we have tested these models on several datasets from the BIOAQS and TREC question answering challenge, finding that they outperform BM-25, PACRR and DRMM.

(1) the best performing models use multiple views of the query and document; (2) the best models are the most complex ones that combine the views of query and documents; and (3) the best models use context-sensitive term encodings.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how to best represent the interactions between queries and documents, and how to best use these interactions to rank documents in terms of their relevance to a given query.

the following questions: How can we improve on the Deep Relevance Ranking Model (DRMM), which is a state-of-the-art model for relevance ranking? Can we improve the performance of PACRR, which is another state-of-the-art deep relevance ranking model? How do we improve on the performance of PACERR?
the question of how to best represent and combine information from query-document term interactions in a neural model.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the proposed models outperform the state-of-the-art models, DRMM and PACRR, on both datasets.
our proposed models outperform BM25, DRMM, PACRR and other baselines on the datasets used.
we propose a novel approach for deep neural network based relevance matching, which outperforms state of the art models on several datasets.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the new models outperformed DRMM by 0.4-0.6 MAP on the TREC dataset, and 0.2-0.3 on the BIOASQ dataset.
the proposed models are able to capture richer document-query interactions, leading to significant improvements on the performance of relevance ranking.

we show how the context-sensitive encodings are useful for the task of document relevance ranking and we show how the deep learning models can be used as a general purpose tool to learn from these encodings.
The main takeaway from our work is that

document-query interactions can be used to learn rich representations of documents that capture both local and global term interactions, and that such representations are more useful than those produced by DRMM or PACRR.
the choice of interaction features is crucial to the performance of neural models for relevance ranking, and that simple extensions of existing models can yield large improvements.
the use of rich, context-sensitive encodings of query and document term interactions is critical for achieving state-of-the-art performance.
